machine learning.definition: A field of artificial intelligence focused on building systems that learn and improve from data without being explicitly programmed for every task.

supervised learning.definition: A machine learning approach where the model learns from labeled training data to make predictions on new, unseen data.

unsupervised learning.definition: A machine learning approach where the model finds patterns in data without labeled examples or target outputs.

self-supervised learning.definition: A machine learning approach where the model learns by predicting parts of the input from other parts, creating supervision signals from the data itself without external labels.

zero-shot learning.definition: The ability of a model to perform a task or classify examples it has never seen during training, typically by leveraging learned representations or instructions.

few-shot learning.definition: The ability of a model to quickly adapt to new tasks with only a few examples, often demonstrated by providing examples in the input prompt.

transfer learning.definition: A machine learning technique where knowledge gained from training on one task is applied to improve performance on a different but related task.

gradient descent.definition: An optimization algorithm that iteratively adjusts model parameters in the direction that minimizes the loss function.

stochastic gradient descent.definition: A variant of gradient descent that updates parameters using gradients computed on small random batches of data rather than the entire dataset.

backpropagation.definition: The algorithm used to calculate gradients in neural networks by propagating errors backward through the network layers.

loss function.definition: A function that measures how well a model's predictions match the actual target values, used to guide training.

overfitting.definition: When a model learns the training data too well, including noise and specific details, leading to poor performance on new data.

underfitting.definition: When a model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data, leading to poor performance on both training and test data.

training set.definition: The portion of data used to train a machine learning model by adjusting its parameters.

validation set.definition: A subset of data used to evaluate model performance during training and tune hyperparameters, separate from the test set.

test set.definition: A subset of data held out from training and validation, used only for final evaluation of model performance.

learning rate.definition: A hyperparameter that controls how much the model parameters are updated during each step of gradient descent.

neural network.definition: A computational model inspired by biological neural networks, consisting of interconnected nodes (neurons) organized in layers.

deep learning.definition: A subset of machine learning using neural networks with multiple hidden layers to learn complex patterns in data.

transformer.definition: A neural network architecture that uses attention mechanisms to process sequential data, particularly effective for language tasks.

softmax.definition: An activation function that converts a vector of real numbers into a probability distribution, commonly used in classification tasks.

batch normalization.definition: A technique that normalizes inputs to each layer, accelerating training and improving model stability.

hyperparameter.definition: A configuration setting that controls the learning process but is not learned from data, such as learning rate or number of layers.

optimizer.definition: An algorithm that updates model parameters based on computed gradients, such as SGD, Adam, or RMSprop.

fine-tuning.definition: The process of taking a pre-trained model and further training it on a specific task or dataset.

pre-training.definition: The initial training phase where a model learns general representations from a large dataset before being adapted to specific tasks.

foundation model.definition: A large-scale model trained on diverse data that serves as a base for adaptation to various downstream tasks, typically through fine-tuning or prompting.

multimodal.definition: Relating to AI systems that can process and understand multiple types of data (such as text, images, audio, video) simultaneously.
